title: Defense: signals, second and third hand, and leading mid-hand

deals.source: Phil Abrahamson, “10 Attitude Signals on Defense”, page 7, case 1

problems.explanation: Partner's ace promises the king. You hold the ♥Q, so partner can cash the K and lead a third heart to your Q: you'd like hearts continued. A high spot card encourages: play the ♥8.

whyNot.H3: A low spot card discourages. Partner might switch, and your side would lose its third heart trick.
whyNot.HQ: Partner's A and K win the first two tricks anyway. Keep the Q to win the third.

deals.source: Phil Abrahamson, “10 Attitude Signals on Defense”, page 7, case 2

problems.explanation: Without the ♥Q, you don't want partner to go on: if declarer has the Q, cashing the K sets it up, but if you wait, declarer may never make it. A low spot card discourages: play the ♥3.

whyNot.H8: A high spot card encourages, and partner would cash the K, setting up declarer's Q.

deals.source: Phil Abrahamson, “10 Attitude Signals on Defense”, page 9

problems.explanation: With two cards, play high then low. The ♥8 encourages: partner cashes the K, you follow with the 3, and partner leads a third heart for you to ruff.

whyNot.H3: Low discourages, and you'd miss the ruff. With a doubleton, play the higher card first.

deals.source: Phil Abrahamson, “10 Attitude Signals on Defense”, page 13, hand 2
reviewNotes: The handout doesn't show dummy; the dummy here is chosen to fit.

problems.explanation: Three small cards and no honor: nothing to encourage. Play your lowest, the ♥3, to discourage.

whyNot.H8: The 8 is a high spot card: it would encourage partner to continue.

deals.source: Phil Abrahamson, “10 Attitude Signals on Defense”, page 13, hand 4
reviewNotes: The handout doesn't show dummy; the dummy here is chosen to fit.

problems.explanation: Partner's ♥K promises the Q, and you have the J: together you hold K Q J, so hearts are safe to continue. Encourage with a high spot card: the ♥8.

whyNot.H3: Low discourages. With the J completing partner's sequence, you want hearts.

deals.source: Phil Abrahamson, “10 Attitude Signals on Defense”, page 13, hand 5
reviewNotes: The handout doesn't show dummy; the dummy here is chosen to fit.

problems.explanation: Partner's ♥Q promises the J. With no honor to help, discourage with your lowest card: the ♥3.

whyNot.H8: A high spot card would ask partner to continue, with nothing to back it up.

deals.source: Phil Abrahamson, “10 Attitude Signals on Defense”, page 13, hand 6
reviewNotes: The handout doesn't show dummy; the dummy here is chosen to fit.

problems.explanation: Partner's ♥Q promises the J, and you have the K: hearts are your side's suit. Encourage with a high spot card, the ♥8, and keep the K.

whyNot.HK: Don't play your K on partner's Q: the Q will win if declarer doesn't take it, and the K is worth keeping.
whyNot.H3: Low discourages, but you want hearts continued.

deals.source: Phil Abrahamson, “10 Attitude Signals on Defense”, page 12

problems.explanation: Signals aren't only for when partner's card wins. Partner's ♦K promises the Q, and dummy took the A. With the ♦J, you know it's safe for partner to continue diamonds later: encourage with the ♦8.

whyNot.D3: Low discourages. Your J makes diamonds a good suit for partner to attack again.

deals.source: Phil Abrahamson, “10 Attitude Signals on Defense”, page 16

problems.explanation: With a doubleton, start high-low: the ♦5, then the 2. The 5 doesn't look high, but partner, seeing the 2 missing, should read it as encouraging, cash the K and give you a ruff.

whyNot.D2: Your lowest card discourages, and you'd miss the ruff. Start a high-low with the 5.

deals.source: Phil Abrahamson, “10 Attitude Signals on Defense”, page 17
reviewNotes: The handout states the rule without an example; the cards here are chosen to fit.

problems.explanation: The exception: with Q x under partner's ace, play the small card. Playing the Q under the ace promises the J (or a singleton), and partner would underlead the K to your 'J'.

whyNot.CQ: The Q under partner's ace shows the J as well, or a singleton. With Q x, play the x.

deals.source: Phil Abrahamson, “10 Attitude Signals on Defense”, page 23

problems.explanation: Think about dummy's ♦Q. If partner continues with the K, the Q becomes good for declarer, who'll throw a loser on it. If partner switches, declarer never makes the Q. So discourage, even with the J: play the ♦2.

whyNot.D8: Encouraging asks partner to cash the K, setting up dummy's Q for a discard.

deals.source: Phil Abrahamson, “10 Attitude Signals on Defense”, page 18
reviewNotes: The handout writes small cards as x; the spot cards here are chosen to keep its point.
In the handout, partner wins this trick with the ♠A; whether declarer would lead the K into it doesn't matter for the discard.

problems.explanation: You can't follow to the spade, so your discard can signal. You'd love partner to lead a heart through dummy's K J to your A Q. A high spot card in a suit asks for it: discard the ♥7.

acceptable.D2: A low spot card says you don't want a suit, which also points partner away from diamonds.

whyNot.H2: A low heart says you don't want hearts: the opposite of what you mean.
whyNot.HA: Throwing the A gives away a sure trick.

deals.source: Phil Abrahamson, “11 Defense – Guidelines”, page 9

problems.explanation: Second hand low. Declarer leads towards dummy's Q: if you play low, declarer's K (if they have it) and dummy's Q can't both win, because your A kills one of them. And if partner has the K, partner takes the Q.

whyNot.HA: Rising with the A sets up both dummy's Q and declarer's K: two tricks instead of one.
whyNot.HJ: Splitting your honors gives declarer a cheap trick. Play low.

deals.source: Phil Abrahamson, “11 Defense – Guidelines”, page 10

problems.explanation: Second hand low, in tempo. If you play low smoothly, declarer has to guess between the K and the J, and may guess wrong. If you hesitate, declarer knows you're thinking about the A and plays the K.

whyNot.HA: Rising with the A sets up dummy's K and J. Keep it to capture an honor later.

deals.source: Phil Abrahamson, “11 Defense – Guidelines”, page 11

problems.explanation: Cover an honor with an honor. If you play low, declarer lets the Q run, then leads towards the A J, and your K dies anyway. Covering kills the Q with your K, and partner's 10 may become a winner.

whyNot.H4: Declarer's Q wins, and your K is caught on the next round.

deals.source: Phil Abrahamson, “11 Defense – Guidelines”, page 13

problems.explanation: Third hand high: you're the last chance to win the trick for your side. Partner led low, so partner doesn't have the K Q. Win the ♥A and lead back to partner's honors: partner may have the K, or the Q sitting over declarer.

whyNot.H9: If declarer has the K or Q, playing low lets declarer win a cheap trick.

deals.source: Phil Abrahamson, “11 Defense – Guidelines”, page 14

problems.explanation: Third hand high: play the ♠Q. Partner led low, so partner doesn't have the A. If declarer takes the Q with the A, partner's K (or J) is set up for later.

whyNot.S9: Declarer could win cheaply with the J or 10.

deals.source: Phil Abrahamson, “11 Defense – Guidelines”, page 15

problems.explanation: Third hand high, but the lowest of touching cards: the ♦10. If declarer wins with the A, partner knows you have the Q and J (declarer would have won with them otherwise), and keeps attacking diamonds.

whyNot.DQ: From touching cards, play the lowest. The Q would tell partner declarer has the J, and partner might stop leading the suit.

deals.source: Phil Abrahamson, “11 Defense – Guidelines”, page 21

problems.explanation: Think before playing third hand high. Partner's ♥J promises the 10, so declarer has the Q. If you take the A now, dummy's K and declarer's Q are both good. Keep the A to kill the K later, and encourage with the ♥9.

whyNot.HA: Winning the A sets up two heart tricks for declarer: dummy's K and the Q.
whyNot.H2: Low discourages, but you want partner to continue hearts through dummy's K.

deals.source: Phil Abrahamson, “10 Attitude Signals on Defense”, page 14, case 1
reviewNotes: The handout gives only the hearts; the other suits are made up to fit.

problems.explanation: Your ♥K won, and partner's ♥8 is a high spot card: it encourages, so partner has the ♥A or the J. Partner wants hearts, so continue: lead the ♥Q, the top of what's left of your K Q.

whyNot.H3: Right suit, and low works when partner has the A. But the Q is safe whoever has it.
whyNot.D2: Partner asked for hearts. A diamond up to dummy's A Q also gives declarer a free finesse.
whyNot.C3: Partner asked for hearts. A club gives up your heart tricks for nothing.

deals.source: Phil Abrahamson, “10 Attitude Signals on Defense”, page 14, case 2
reviewNotes: The handout gives only the hearts and says not to continue them; the rest of the hands, and the club switch, are made up to fit.

problems.explanation: Partner's ♥2 discourages: no ♥Q. If declarer has it, cashing your K sets the Q up as a winner, so leave hearts for partner to lead through it later. Switch instead, and with dummy on your left, lead through dummy's strength: a club through the A Q 10, in case partner has the K or J sitting over them. In the middle of the hand, starting a new suit, we lead BOSTON: bottom of something, top of nothing. With nothing in clubs, lead the top: the ♣7. (On opening lead it's different: from small cards you'd lead low.)

whyNot.C4: The right suit, but a low card says you have an honor in clubs. From nothing, lead the top.
whyNot.C3: The right suit, but a low card says you have an honor in clubs. From nothing, lead the top.
whyNot.HK: Partner's low heart says partner doesn't have the Q. If declarer has it, the K sets it up.
whyNot.DJ: Dummy's diamonds are weak and on your left: a diamond goes round to declarer, who plays last and can win cheaply over partner's honors.

deals.source: Phil Abrahamson, “10 Attitude Signals on Defense”, page 14, case 4
reviewNotes: The handout gives only the hearts; the other suits are made up to fit.

problems.explanation: Partner's ♥2 discourages, but partner can't see your hand: it only says partner has nothing in hearts. You know the K and Q are both winners. A signal is information, not an order: when you know more, act on it. Cash your hearts before declarer can throw them away.

acceptable.HQ: The same: the K and Q are both winners.

whyNot.D5: Partner's low heart doesn't ask for a switch when you hold the K and Q. Take your tricks.
whyNot.C6: Partner's low heart doesn't ask for a switch when you hold the K and Q. Take your tricks.

deals.source: Phil Abrahamson, “10 Attitude Signals on Defense”, page 24
reviewNotes: The handout gives only the hearts; the other suits are made up to fit.

problems.explanation: Partner's ♥3 doesn't encourage, so partner has no Q, and it isn't the start of a high-low, so partner doesn't have a doubleton. That leaves two cases. Partner has a singleton: cash the K, then give partner a ruff. Or partner has three or more without the Q: then declarer has only the Q left, and it falls under your K. Either way, continue with the K.

whyNot.H4: If declarer's last heart is the Q, a low heart lets it win. Cash the K and it falls.
whyNot.D2: Switching gives up the ruff, or the Q falling under your K. Partner's low heart is information to think about, not an order to switch.

deals.source: Phil Abrahamson, “10 Attitude Signals on Defense”, page 25
reviewNotes: The handout's dummy shows small cards as x; the spots, and the hearts played to trick 1 other than the A and 8, are made up to fit.

problems.explanation: Partner's ♥8 encourages: partner has the Q. (It can't be the start of a doubleton: declarer would have six hearts and would have opened 1♥.) Once declarer gets in, trumps get drawn and the diamond losers go on dummy's clubs, so you need four tricks now: two hearts and two diamonds. Declarer has the ♦K for the opening bid, and if you lead diamonds you set it up. So lead your low heart to partner's Q, and partner, looking at dummy, switches to a diamond through declarer's K to your A Q.

whyNot.HK: You make two hearts, but then you have to lead diamonds yourself, or a third heart that declarer may ruff. Partner needs to be on lead, to lead diamonds through the K.
whyNot.DA: One diamond trick, and declarer's K is then a winner. You need partner to lead through it.
whyNot.DQ: Declarer wins the K. Diamonds have to come from partner, through declarer.
whyNot.C8: Dummy's clubs are solid: once declarer is in, they'll take care of declarer's losers. Act now.

deals.setAside: The same point as hand3-save-ace, from the same page (2026-11-06).
deals.source: Phil Abrahamson, “11 Defense: Guidelines”, page 21

problems.explanation: Partner's ♦J is the top of a sequence: it promises the 10 and denies the Q (from Q J 10, partner would lead the Q). So declarer has the Q. Take your A now and declarer's K and Q are both winners. Keep the A to capture dummy's K later. A singleton Q with declarer would give partner seven diamonds, and partner would have bid. Thinking beats the guideline here: don't play third hand high. Play the 9, a high spot, to say you like diamonds.

whyNot.DA: Third hand high, but here it sets up declarer's K and Q. Keep the A for dummy's K.
whyNot.D2: Ducking is right, but the 2 discourages. The 9 tells partner you like diamonds, so partner leads them again, through dummy's K.

deals.source: Phil Abrahamson, “11 Defense: Guidelines”, page 18
reviewNotes: The handout gives dummy's spades, hearts and diamonds; your hand is made up to fit, with no heart or diamond honors, so the guideline decides.

problems.explanation: Dummy is on your left, so lead through dummy's strength: a heart through the A Q 10. Dummy has to play before partner, so if partner has the K or J, partner can wait to pounce on whatever dummy plays. In the middle of the hand, starting a new suit, we lead BOSTON: bottom of something, top of nothing. With nothing in hearts, lead the top: the ♥8. (On opening lead it's different: from small cards you'd lead low.)

whyNot.H7: The right suit, but lead the top from nothing: the 8.
whyNot.H4: The right suit, but a low card says you have an honor in hearts. From nothing, lead the top.
whyNot.D9: Dummy's diamonds are small and on your left: a diamond goes round to declarer, who plays last and can win cheaply over partner's honors.
whyNot.C3: Dummy has no clubs: declarer ruffs in dummy and throws a loser from hand, a ruff and discard. Don't give one.

deals.source: Phil Abrahamson, “11 Defense: Guidelines”, page 19
reviewNotes: The handout gives dummy's spades, hearts and diamonds; your hand is made up to fit.

problems.explanation: Dummy is on your right, so lead the weakest thing in sight: a diamond, up to dummy's small ones. Partner's diamonds sit behind declarer's, and partner can see dummy has nothing, so partner knows exactly what to play. Starting a new suit in the middle of the hand, lead the top of an honor sequence if you have one: from J 10 8 7, the J.

whyNot.D7: The right suit, but with an honor sequence, lead its top: the J.
whyNot.H9: A heart goes round to dummy's A Q 10, and dummy plays last: whatever partner has, declarer can win it cheaply. That's a free finesse.
whyNot.C9: Dummy has no clubs: declarer ruffs in dummy and throws a loser from hand, a ruff and discard. Don't give one.

deals.source: Phil Abrahamson, “11 Defense: Guidelines”, page 20
reviewNotes: Made up to apply page 20's rhyme, "If dummy's on your left, lead through heft", when your other suits have honors in them.

problems.explanation: Dummy is on your left, so lead through its strength: a diamond through the K Q 10, in case partner has the A or J over them. Your hearts and clubs are worse leads: dummy's cards there are small, and declarer plays last, so leading away from your K or Q gives declarer a free finesse. In the middle of the hand, starting a new suit, we lead BOSTON: bottom of something, top of nothing. With nothing in diamonds, lead the top: the ♦8. (On opening lead it's different: from small cards you'd lead low.)

whyNot.D6: The right suit, but lead the top from nothing: the 8.
whyNot.D5: The right suit, but a low card says you have an honor in diamonds. From nothing, lead the top.
whyNot.D2: The right suit, but a low card says you have an honor in diamonds. From nothing, lead the top.
whyNot.H4: Away from your K, round to declarer, who plays last: if declarer has the A Q, you've given away a trick.
whyNot.C5: Away from your Q, round to declarer, who plays last: a free finesse.
